pulls.title: Adjust description of W3C
pulls.author: dontcallmedom
pulls.body: I've started reviewing the doc as I was pointed to it by a colleague; I'm planning to conduct a more in depth review, but meanwhile, I hope this is a useful simple contribution

reviews.author: tarakiyee
reviews.body:
Thanks Dom, and apologies for the slow response, this sat longer than it should have. Glad to have your eyes on this, and I'd very much welcome the deeper review.

On the change: I think we'll have to drop the global because all the SDOs mentioned are global too. Adding the facts that the W3C patent policy is royalty-free and the horizontal review structure is a great improvement to the description. 

I would push back against two terms however, namely "vendor-neutral" and "rigorous." This guide describes standards bodies from an external evaluator's voice rather than each institution's own voice. W3C is a fee-based membership consortium, and the membership structure would be important to highlight to prospective funders, so I want to keep it visible here. And whether horizontal review is rigorous is an assessment thing, I'd rather state the fact that it's a formal process.

I would suggest the following change: 

> **W3C**: Membership-based consortium for web standards with a royalty-free patent policy, with a formal horizontal review process covering accessibility, internationalization, privacy, and security.

If that looks good to you, let me know. And thank you for catching that typo!

pulls.title: Emphasize funding participants who can engage on the venue's terms
pulls.author: tarakiyee
pulls.body: Address review feedback: in an IETF context, funding people with both the technical and social skills to engage successfully is far more effective than funding participation from a purely user or advocacy perspective, however much one might wish the venue worked otherwise. Added as the leading point under Supporting Public Interest Participation.

pulls.title: Ground cultural rights and i18n evaluation in RFC 6365
pulls.author: tarakiyee
pulls.body: Address review feedback: the cultural rights discussion referenced linguistic rights without any technical anchor. Cite RFC 6365 in both the ESC rights section and the Accessibility and Inclusion criteria, including the internationalization/localization distinction.

pulls.title: Add concrete examples of timescales and topic spillover
pulls.author: tarakiyee
pulls.body: Address review feedback: add examples emphasizing how long standards work takes and how successful engagement in one topic grows into involvement in others. The pervasive monitoring / DNS encryption arc (RFC 7258 -> RFC 7858 -> RFC 8484 -> ECH) illustrates decade-plus timescales; MLS (RFC 9420) -> MIMI illustrates five years per protocol and the compounding of expertise across adjacent work.

pulls.title: Add environmental impact as a top-level consideration
pulls.author: tarakiyee
pulls.body: Address review feedback: add environmental impact alongside human rights and social impact, drawing on RFC 9547 (IAB workshop report) and the IAB E-Impact program. Framed as a funding opportunity: the absence of established assessment methodologies is exactly the kind of gap public investment can fill.

pulls.title: Expand sustained engagement into its own subsection
pulls.author: tarakiyee
pulls.body: Address review feedback: the single closing paragraph undersold the guide's most important practical warning. Break it into three claims (timescales, trust/reputation, process literacy) with funding implications for each, and add a subsection on working with experienced communities, echoed in the capacity building recommendations.

pulls.title: Cite Cath (2021) and Castka & Balzarova (2008)
pulls.author: tarakiyee
pulls.body: Address review feedback: add two literature references. Cath's ethnography of human rights advocacy in the IETF turns the guide's 'openness in principle vs. practice' argument into a documented finding, cited in both the Open Process section and the human rights background. The ISO 26000 diffusion paper gives the standards organizations section a documented non-IETF case.

pulls.title: Add concentrated control as a fifth market failure
pulls.author: tarakiyee
pulls.body: Address review feedback: public funding to standardize a technology against monopoly control is a distinct market failure - the dominant party benefits from non-standardization.

pulls.title: Write the Success Metrics section
pulls.author: tarakiyee
pulls.body: Replace the TODO with a metrics framework differentiated by funding mode (development / participation / impact assessment), based on the Osborne, Sharratt, Foster and Boehm toolkit for measuring impacts of public funding on open source (arXiv:2411.06027) and mapped onto the guide's existing RFC anchors (7942, 6410, 7282, 6973, 9620). Includes warnings on metric gaming and on the standards-stock vs participation funding distinction.
